As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece. These cultures believed that the sky was a dome above the Earth, and that the stars and planets were gods or spirits.

The ancient Greeks, in particular, were fascinated by the night sky and made detailed observations of the stars and planets. They believed that the Earth was surrounded by a crystal sphere, and that the stars and planets were attached to this sphere. This idea was later challenged by the ancient Greek philosopher Aristarchus of Samos, who proposed a heliocentric model of the solar system.

The modern understanding of outer space as a vast, dark void was developed during the 16th and 17th centuries, with the work of astronomers such as Copernicus, Galileo, and Kepler. These scientists used telescopes to study the night sky and made observations that challenged the geocentric model of the universe.

The idea that space outside of Earth's atmosphere was blue as the morning sky is a misconception that has been debunked by scientists. The color of space is actually black, as it absorbs all wavelengths of light. The stars and galaxies that we see in the night sky are actually very far away, and their light takes thousands or even millions of years to reach us.

The misconception about the color of space may have originated from the fact that the Earth's atmosphere scatters sunlight in a way that makes the sky appear blue during the day. This scattering effect is known as Rayleigh scattering, and it is responsible for the blue color of the sky. However, this effect does not apply to space, which is a vacuum and does not scatter light in the same way.

In summary, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years, and our understanding of the universe has evolved over time through the work of many scientists and astronomers. The idea that space is blue as the morning sky is a misconception that has been debunked by scientists, and we now know that space is actually a vast, dark void that is illuminated only by the light of stars and galaxies.
